Definition: from G243 and ἀγορέω (to harangue (compare G58)); to allegorize:--be an allegory (the Greek word itself).
BiblicalUsage: Once, when Paul reads the story of Hagar and Sarah as an allegory: which things are an allegory, for these are the two covenants, the one from the mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage, which is Agar. The word is the allegorizing itself, the reading of a history as a picture of something greater.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for allegorizing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the reading it names, that Paul found two covenants in two mothers and built his whole argument on it.
